o: A special substring contains every character that appears in it entirely (no occurrence outside), and is not the whole string. We must decide whether k disjoint special substrings can be picked. Key reduction: a special substring starting at l must extend at least to r = max(last[c]) over characters in s[l..r] (a closure), and is valid only if every character inside has first[c] ≥ l. Crucially, a valid special substring can only START at a position l where first[s[l]] == l — otherwise the character s[l] appears earlier, violating the rule. There are at most 26 such positions, so we generate at most 26 minimal candidate intervals and run classic activity selection (greedy by right endpoint) to maximize disjoint picks. Example 1 yields candidates "cd" and "ef" → true for k=2; example 2 yields only "e","f" → false for k=3.
k: Any special substring can be shrunk to the minimal closure interval starting at the same index, so only minimal candidates matter.
Valid starts satisfy first[s[l]] == l, giving at most 26 candidates.
Maximum disjoint intervals = greedy by earliest right endpoint.

a.i: For each of the ≤26 positions l with first[s[l]]==l, expand r until stable (r = max last-position of seen chars); accept if no char's first occurrence precedes l and the interval isn't the whole string. Then greedily pick non-overlapping intervals sorted by right end.
s: Record first[c], last[c] for each letter.
For each valid start l, compute the closure interval [l, r].
Keep accepted candidates, sort by r, greedily count disjoint intervals.
a.t: O(26·n) — at most 26 closure computations, each linear; sorting ≤26 intervals.

w: The two reductions (shrink to minimal closure; only ≤26 legal starts) are what interviewers look for. Pitfalls: don't forget the whole-string exclusion, k=0 returns true, and the first-occurrence check. Follow-up: return the actual substrings, or handle k larger than 26 (immediately false).
